claims.text: For women of the gentry, education and paid work were extremely limited, so marriage was close to a necessity. Austen herself wrote that single women have a dreadful propensity for being poor.

citations.title: The Marriage Law of Jane Austen’s World
citations.author: Martha Bailey
citations.quote: Educational and employment opportunities for women were extremely limited. Marriage was almost a necessity.

claims.text: Once married, a wife lost her separate legal identity, and her husband became entitled to her property and income, unless a marriage settlement protected it.

citations.title: The Marriage Law of Jane Austen’s World
citations.author: Martha Bailey
citations.quote: One implication of coverture was that the husband became entitled to his wife’s property and income.

claims.text: Families tried to keep a landed estate intact by passing it to the eldest son or the nearest male relative, often by a legal arrangement called an entail. Daughters and younger sons were left dependent on relatives.

citations.title: The Marriage Law of Jane Austen’s World
citations.author: Martha Bailey
citations.quote: The purpose of favoring the eldest son, either by application of the law of primogeniture or by wills or settlements, was to keep family estates intact and free of heavy obligations to support other family members.

claims.text: The novel's Bennet family is caught by this practice: the settlement of the family property prevents Mr. Bennet from providing for his wife and daughters after his death. That is why finding husbands for five daughters is so urgent.

citations.title: The Marriage Law of Jane Austen’s World
citations.author: Martha Bailey
citations.quote: The settlement of the family property prevents Mr. Bennet from providing for his wife and daughters after his death.

items.heading: War with France and the militia

claims.text: Britain was at war with France for most of the two decades after 1793. Each county raised a militia, a part-time home-defence force officered by men of property, whose main job was to guard against French invasion.

citations.title: Jane Austen's brother and the Royal Oxfordshire Militia mutiny of 1795
citations.author: Brighton & Hove Museums
citations.quote: Militia were reserve military forces, a little like the present day Territorial Army.

citations.title: Jane Austen's brother and the Royal Oxfordshire Militia mutiny of 1795
citations.author: Brighton & Hove Museums
citations.quote: The primary purpose of these milita was to provide protection against French invasion.

claims.text: Militia regiments were quartered in and around towns and in seaside camps, which is why red-coated officers are a social presence in the book's Hertfordshire neighbourhood and in the Brighton of its later chapters.

citations.title: Jane Austen's brother and the Royal Oxfordshire Militia mutiny of 1795
citations.author: Brighton & Hove Museums
citations.quote: Henry’s experiences almost certainly informed the descriptions of Brighton that appear in Pride & Prejudice

items.heading: Written young, revised in middle age

claims.text: Austen drafted the book in her early twenties in the Steventon rectory, then rewrote it after moving to Chawton in 1809, once she was preparing her early manuscripts for publication.

citations.title: How 'First Impressions' became 'Pride and Prejudice'...
citations.author: Jane Austen's House
citations.quote: When Jane arrived in Chawton in 1809, she took out her early manuscripts and set to work rewriting them for publication.

claims.text: She changed the title partly because another novel called First Impressions, by Margaret Holford, had appeared in 1801.

citations.title: How 'First Impressions' became 'Pride and Prejudice'...
citations.author: Jane Austen's House
citations.quote: Since drafting First Impressions, another novel with that name had appeared, by Margaret Holford, published in 1801.

claims.text: Sense and Sensibility, published by Thomas Egerton in 1811 with help from her brother Henry, came first. With Henry's help she also secured Egerton as publisher for Pride and Prejudice, which came out on 28 January 1813.

citations.title: How 'First Impressions' became 'Pride and Prejudice'...
citations.author: Jane Austen's House
citations.quote: With help from her brother Henry, Jane secured a publishing contract with Thomas Egerton and Pride and Prejudice was published on 28 January 1813.

claims.text: The day after publication she wrote to her sister Cassandra about receiving her 'own darling Child' from London. She also said she had 'lopt & cropt' the text so that it was shorter than Sense and Sensibility.

citations.title: How 'First Impressions' became 'Pride and Prejudice'...
citations.author: Jane Austen's House
citations.quote: I have lopt & cropt so successfully however that I imagine it must be rather shorter than S&S. altogether.

claims.text: A legal settlement fixing who inherits an estate, usually a male heir, so that the current owner cannot leave it to his daughters.

citations.title: The Marriage Law of Jane Austen’s World
citations.author: Martha Bailey
citations.quote: Settlements of property, often made on the occasion of a marriage, typically gave the husband a life interest in the estate, and the property would be entailed on the eldest son (or other male descendant)

claims.text: A county-raised reserve force, not required to serve overseas, officered by property owners; its regiments were stationed around England during the wars with France.

claims.text: Younger sons of landed families inherited little and had to enter a profession such as the army, the church or the law; this made it harder for them to marry.

citations.title: The Marriage Law of Jane Austen’s World
citations.author: Martha Bailey
citations.quote: Younger sons as well as daughters suffered under the general preference for eldest sons.
